title: Newer specialized pre-play material overrides a stale aggregate line
question: Was Golden Dawn player membership a live adaptation?
evidence: One aggregate line says The Golden Dawn: NPC ONLY.
The latest available pre-opening W1 revision says travelers may be sponsored by one of four patron groups and each patron interviews potential player groups.
It schedules Golden Dawn Quest by DM Rob and says Golden Dawn operatives know about the sabotage and are encouraged to delay the fight.
finding: The contradiction existed before opening. The specialized W1 run document already treats Golden Dawn as player-facing, so no player-caused change is required to explain live membership.
judgment: WHEN sources conflict, prefer the dated, specialized document closest to actual play over a stale aggregate instruction unless live evidence shows the older rule was deliberately restored. Do not manufacture an adaptation story from contradictory prep.

title: A prep audit restores a storyline that schedule editing accidentally erased
question: What makes Brendon change preparation before players encounter it?
evidence: Brendon notices schedule fiddling removed the Tatankan storyline, decides to cover it with a mini-drama across Week 4, then designs Sorrow and Tatankan puzzles.
Week 4 now contains a Tatankan escape-room thread, a red flare at the Pen, and a later return to the Pen.
Brendon deploys the prepared red-flare signal at the Tatankan pen and announces the Sorrow of the Stones side challenge.
finding: This change predates player contact by months. The trigger was Brendon's own coverage audit: a desired through-line disappeared while the schedule was being rearranged.
judgment: IF revision work accidentally removes a story function the campaign still needs, THEN restore that function with the smallest coherent through-line and seed it early enough to feel native. Classify this as prep-driven even if players later engage with it.

title: An abstract DM tool is invented during prep, then used as a live adjudication primitive
question: How does Brendon turn a design problem into a repeatable DM mechanic?
evidence: Brendon writes New DM Function: Group Checks and defines success as at least half the party succeeding, with harder thresholds for harder tasks.
During live play, Brendon offers a contested Strength group check and explicitly says at least half of the people pushing back must pass.
finding: The live mechanic is a pre-play tool created to solve a recurring multiplayer adjudication problem, then reused when the fiction matches.
judgment: WHEN a recurring table situation is awkward to adjudicate case-by-case, THEN extract a simple reusable procedure during prep and later invoke it only when the fiction matches the problem it was built to solve.

title: Roleplay prompts are deliberately added as infrastructure, then used to focus communal play
question: Does Brendon rely on spontaneous social play, or build tools to provoke it?
evidence: Brendon records that he peppered in Group Prompts as a new way to encourage roleplay.
Brendon posts a Group Prompt telling players to gather at the pub to discuss who should be tyrant mayor and what the mayor should do.
finding: He does not wait for every social scene to self-start. He creates lightweight scaffolds that point players at a shared question without deciding the answer.
judgment: IF the campaign needs player-to-player roleplay around a common issue, THEN create a prompt that supplies topic, location, and immediate social purpose while leaving positions and outcome to the players.

title: Feeling that prep is sparse triggers a missing-pillar audit, not more generic prose
question: What makes Brendon decide preparation is not working?
evidence: Brendon diagnoses why material feels sparse: We aren't designing combat encounters in the fluff. He starts a bestiary and searches owned content for monsters.
Subsequent Week 4 prep adds actionable monster material such as Mothmen warnings and Halfwudgie riders tied to later consequences.
finding: The diagnosis targets a missing form of play, not the amount of prose. The corrective action adds encounters and usable monster hooks.
judgment: WHEN prep feels thin, THEN diagnose which form of play is absent before writing more. Add playable decisions, opposition, interaction, discovery, or reward according to the missing function rather than increasing descriptive volume.

title: Player pursuit triggers a just-in-time high-stakes branch minutes before delivery
question: What does a real player-caused prep mutation look like in the revision record?
evidence: Kvatch contains the painted-over door and clue infrastructure, but not the later hard-mode ending.
A player goes to the Kvatch Hatch for solitude.
The player recognizes that the Hatch is spelling something and recruits Dorfin to investigate.
The document adds BFDM on hard mode, a first-ending branch, a five-player Sibriex/Croatoan fight, real character death, and the swordfish reader trigger.
Brendon posts the newly added hard-mode branch four minutes after the revision.
A player immediately accepts by replying Swordfish.
finding: The base mystery was prepared. The extreme branch appears only after a player actively re-engages the location, then is delivered four minutes later. The timing strongly supports just-in-time expansion of the touched thread.
judgment: IF players push on a prepared mystery harder than the prepared depth supports, THEN deepen the existing object in place when doing so preserves its identity and creates a worthwhile choice. Prefer extending the thing they touched over diverting them to unrelated content.

title: A live document edit can be an operational delivery edit rather than a story adaptation
question: How do we avoid treating every during-play revision as evidence that players changed the story?
evidence: The barkeep instruction is tightened to: The role of week 3 barkeep can be claimed by an aristocrat. Weeks 4 and 5 will be assigned.
Brendon posts essentially the same instruction to everyone about 14 seconds later.
finding: The edit is immediately mirrored into player-facing communication. Nothing in the evidence establishes a new story branch or response to player behavior; it is runtime clarification/administration.
judgment: WHEN a live revision is followed almost immediately by matching player-facing text and contains no new causal branch, classify it as operational delivery unless other evidence links it to player behavior.

title: Most Week 1 live edits are maintenance, proving edit-time alone is a weak causality signal
question: What is the baseline rate of harmless during-play editing?
evidence: Opening pledge changes the destination of a dead traveler's possessions from remains to effects.
Day labels and Saturday/Sunday location text are corrected; museum posting text is added.
Event title is cleaned from Billy the Render 2 Electric boogaloo to Billy the Render 2; small day-label corrections occur.
A Kraken/tentacle sentence is split into description plus a clearer mechanical line without changing the encounter concept.
finding: Week 1 was edited repeatedly while live, but surviving text deltas are predominantly corrections, copy changes, and clearer delivery. Edited during play cannot by itself mean player-caused adaptation.
judgment: Require a causal bridge before labeling a live revision as emergent DM judgment: a player signal before the edit, a meaningful semantic change, and preferably downstream use connected to that signal.

title: Major live adaptation often happens outside the canonical week document
question: Does Brendon rewrite the master plan every time the campaign adapts?
evidence: No paragraph-text delta was detected between the last pre-play Week 4 revision and its only available live Week 4 revision.
Before Week 4 starts, Brendon says he withheld the whole cure because he asked to tie it into awakening the Tatankans.
The campaign is actively deploying Tatankan/Sorrow side material during Week 4.
finding: The formal Week 4 text is stable while connective tissue is negotiated and deployed in Discord. Brendon's adaptation layer is partly external to the canonical schedule.
judgment: DO NOT equate change prep with edit the campaign document. Runtime adaptation can be additive and external: preserve a stable spine while attaching local branches and consequences in the live medium.

title: Adaptive slack in Week 5 was designed before play, then filled from accumulated history
question: Was player-led Week 5 an emergency improvisation or a design choice?
evidence: The outline has seven named daily main events, explicitly reserves Day 33 for Invitationals, and leaves many time blocks open.
The master schedule likewise places Invitationals on Day 33 between major finale beats.
Brendon asks players to DM him the things they want to explore or accomplish going forward.
He explains that Week 5 is much less written so players can lead and DMs can accommodate more invitationals.
finding: Week 5 was not suddenly decompressed after four weeks; adaptive capacity was deliberately reserved months earlier. Live history supplies what fills that reserved space.
judgment: WHEN later campaign history is expected to be more informative than early speculation, reserve low-density slots before play. During play, fill that slack from demonstrated player priorities rather than pre-authoring every minute.

title: Brendon distinguishes missing content from missing function
question: What kind of self-review produces useful revisions?
evidence: Brendon counts 280 possible four-hour slots, subtracts main/voice events, clue scenes, and free-play slots, then concludes that location consolidation and populated NPCs are prerequisites to filling the rest intelligently.
Later audits identify specific lost or missing functions: Tatankan through-line, group RP prompts, and combat encounters inside fluff.
finding: The repeated behavior is not write until full. He inventories what the campaign must support, notices absent functions, then creates targeted structures.
judgment: WHEN preparation feels incomplete, inventory playable functions and dependencies before adding content. Ask what the current material cannot yet do at the table, then repair that capability.

title: Causal classification requires chronology plus semantic change plus a live trigger
question: How should future corpus extraction decide whether a revision teaches Brendon-style adaptation?
evidence: Many during-play edits are maintenance and copy changes.
A live edit can be a near-immediate operational script update.
A live edit can also be a substantive new branch appearing between player pursuit and delivery.
A later live payoff can come from a prep-driven correction made months before players see it.
finding: Timestamp alone cannot identify cause. The same edited-during-play bucket covers typo fixes, operational announcements, and true emergent branching.
judgment: Label revisions with at least PREP_DRIVEN, LIVE_OPERATIONAL, LIVE_RESPONSE, and UNRESOLVED/MIXED. Require chronology, meaningful semantic delta, and evidence of the triggering condition before asserting LIVE_RESPONSE. Prefer UNRESOLVED to invented causality.
